q: For any trapped sample of gas, we can measure its temperature ($T$), the volume ($V$) of the space it occupies, its pressure ($P$) against the confining wall and its mass ($m$).
e: True. For any trapped sample of gas, we can measure its temperature (T), the volume (V) of the space it occupies, its pressure (P) against the confining wall and its mass (m). Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws.

q: For any trapped sample of gas, we can measure its temperature ($T$), the volume ($V$), its pressure ($P$) and its colour ($c$).
e: False. For any trapped sample of gas, we can measure its temperature (T), the volume (V) of the space it occupies, its pressure (P) against the confining wall and its mass (m). q: The units of temperature are degree Celsius, degree Fahrenheit and Kelvin.
e: True. The units of temperature are degree Celsius, degree Fahrenheit and Kelvin. Gas laws use Kelvin because that scale starts at absolute zero, where particle motion would stop.

q: The units of temperature are degree Celsius, degree Fahrenheit and Joule.
e: False. The units of temperature are degree Celsius, degree Fahrenheit and Kelvin.

q: The boiling point of water is $100^{\circ}\text{C}$, $212^{\circ}\text{F}$, and $373\text{K}$.
e: True. The boiling point of water is 100^ degreesC, 212^ degreesF, and 373K.

q: The boiling point of water is $100^{\circ}\text{C}$, $212^{\circ}\text{F}$, and $273\text{K}$.
e: False. The boiling point of water is 100^ degreesC, 212^ degreesF, and 373K.

q: Normal human body temperature is $37^{\circ}\text{C}$, $98.6^{\circ}\text{F}$, and $310\text{K}$.
e: True. Normal human body temperature is 37^ degreesC, 98.6^ degreesF, and 310K.

q: Normal human body temperature is $37^{\circ}\text{C}$, $98.6^{\circ}\text{F}$, and $273\text{K}$.
e: False. Normal human body temperature is 37^ degreesC, 98.6^ degreesF, and 310K.

q: Absolute zero is $-273^{\circ}\text{C}$, $-459.4^{\circ}\text{F}$, and $0\text{K}$.
e: True. Absolute zero is -273^ degreesC, -459.4^ degreesF, and 0K. Absolute zero is 0 K, the point where gas volume in Charles's law would theoretically hit zero.

q: Absolute zero is $0^{\circ}\text{C}$, $0^{\circ}\text{F}$, and $273\text{K}$.
e: False. Absolute zero is -273^ degreesC, -459.4^ degreesF, and 0K. Absolute zero is 0 K, the point where gas volume in Charles's law would theoretically hit zero.

q: The units of volume and their relations are $1000\text{cm}^3 = 1000\text{mL} = 1\text{L} = 1\text{dm}^3$.
e: True. The units of volume and their relations are 1000cm^3 = 1000mL = 1L = 1dm^3. One litre is the same volume as one cubic decimetre, which is also 1000 mL or 1000 cm3.

q: The units of volume and their relations are $100\text{cm}^3 = 100\text{mL} = 1\text{L} = 1\text{dm}^3$.
e: False. The units of volume and their relations are 1000cm^3 = 1000mL = 1L = 1dm^3. One litre is the same volume as one cubic decimetre, which is also 1000 mL or 1000 cm3.

q: A gas exerts a force on the walls of any container.
e: True. A gas exerts a force on the walls of any container. A gas has no shape or volume of its own, so it takes the shape and volume of its container.

q: A gas exerts a force only on the bottom of any container.
e: False. A gas exerts a force on the walls of any container. A gas has no shape or volume of its own, so it takes the shape and volume of its container.

q: Pressure is in fact the force that acts on a given area.
e: True. Pressure is in fact the force that acts on a given area. Gas pressure is the force of collisions on a unit area of the wall.

q: Pressure is in fact the mass that acts on a given volume.
e: False. Pressure is in fact the force that acts on a given area.

q: Force is equal to mass multiplied by acceleration ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2} = \text{N}$).
e: True. Force is equal to mass multiplied by acceleration (kg · m · s^-2 = N). Force is mass multiplied by acceleration, F = ma.

q: Force is equal to mass divided by acceleration.
e: False. Force is equal to mass multiplied by acceleration (kg · m · s^-2 = N). Force is mass multiplied by acceleration, F = ma.

q: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal ($\text{Pa}$), where $1\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^{-2} = 1\text{Pa}$.
e: True. The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), where 1N · m^-2 = 1Pa. The SI unit of pressure is the pascal, one newton per square metre.

q: The SI unit of pressure is the newton ($\text{N}$), where $1\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^{-2} = 1\text{N}$.
e: False. The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), where 1N · m^-2 = 1Pa.

q: Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted on a surface by the air above it as gravity pulls it to the Earth.
e: True. Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted on a surface by the air above it as gravity pulls it to the Earth. Gas pressure is the force of collisions on a unit area of the wall.

q: Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted on a surface by the air below it as gravity pushes it away from the Earth.
e: False. Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted on a surface by the air above it as gravity pulls it to the Earth. Gas pressure is the force of collisions on a unit area of the wall.

q: Instruments used for measuring atmospheric pressure and gas pressure are barometer and manometer, respectively.
e: True. Instruments used for measuring atmospheric pressure and gas pressure are barometer and manometer, respectively. A barometer measures atmospheric pressure, and a manometer measures the pressure of a confined gas.

q: Instruments used for measuring atmospheric pressure and gas pressure are manometer and barometer, respectively.
e: False. Instruments used for measuring atmospheric pressure and gas pressure are barometer and manometer, respectively. A barometer measures atmospheric pressure, and a manometer measures the pressure of a confined gas.

q: Standard atmospheric pressure ($1\text{ atm}$) is equal to the pressure that supports a column of mercury exactly $760\text{ mm}$ high at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ at sea level.
e: True. Standard atmospheric pressure (1 atm) is equal to the pressure that supports a column of mercury exactly 760 mm high at 0^ degreesC at sea level. One atmosphere is 101325 pascals, newtons per square metre.

q: Standard atmospheric pressure ($1\text{ atm}$) is equal to the pressure that supports a column of mercury exactly $760\text{ mm}$ high at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ at sea level.
e: False. Standard atmospheric pressure (1 atm) is equal to the pressure that supports a column of mercury exactly 760 mm high at 0^ degreesC at sea level. One atmosphere is 101325 pascals, newtons per square metre.

q: $1\text{ atm} = 760\text{ mmHg} = 760\text{ torr} = 101,325\text{ Pa} = 101.325\text{ kPa}$.
e: True. 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 101,325 Pa = 101.325 kPa. The torr is defined to be equal to one millimetre of mercury.

q: $1\text{ atm} = 760\text{ mmHg} = 760\text{ torr} = 10,325\text{ Pa}$.
e: False. 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 101,325 Pa = 101.325 kPa. The torr is defined to be equal to one millimetre of mercury.

q: The mass of a gas can be determined by weighing the gas in an enclosed container by gram ($\text{g}$) or kilogram ($\text{kg}$).
e: True. The mass of a gas can be determined by weighing the gas in an enclosed container by gram (g) or kilogram (kg). A gas has no shape or volume of its own, so it takes the shape and volume of its container. The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram, symbol kg.

q: The mass of a gas can be determined by weighing the gas in an open container by gram ($\text{g}$) or kilogram ($\text{kg}$).
e: False. The mass of a gas can be determined by weighing the gas in an enclosed container by gram (g) or kilogram (kg). A gas has no shape or volume of its own, so it takes the shape and volume of its container. The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram, symbol kg.
